<reason>B wins through clearer causal reasoning and more direct engagement. A identifies genuine costs involving incidental civic discovery and classification errors, but overstates reduced recommendations as civic silence and never establishes the claimed polarization effect. B acknowledges those costs while explaining the benefit of avoiding unwanted recommendation loops. B also answers both pressure questions directly. A's unspecified ranking reform does not establish its claimed superiority, especially when B explains that reform and opt-in are compatible.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B decisively answers A's repeated claim that leaving engagement-driven ranking intact means the policy fixes nothing: reducing exposure to a harmful mechanism is itself a benefit. A continues asserting no benefit rather than weighing avoided inflammatory recommendations against lost useful discoveries.</best_rebuttal>
